criterion_notes.c1: Broad encyclopedia overview of environmental health concerns in Uganda (covering malaria, respiratory illness, schistosomiasis, solid waste, industrial effluent, air pollution, heavy metals in soil and vegetables, climate change, and general environmental/food-safety policy). Although it briefly cites aggregate national and Kampala safe-water, piped-water, and sewerage coverage statistics in a subsection on diarrheal disease and mentions the 1996 national water policy in passing, it does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access as a research focus.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the 'Policies, Responses, and Actions' section descriptively summarizes macro-level environmental, occupational health, and food safety frameworks (NEAP, NEMP, NEMA, National Environment Act 1995, EIAs, Factories Act, Public Health Act) and briefly mentions the 1996 national water policy and Directorate of Water Development, without examining how any legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance factor affects water or sanitation access. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, there is no analysis of any rule-type mechanism governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariffs or cost-recovery rules, discretion, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure); the policy discussion is unanalysed macro-governance background.
criterion_notes.c3: Encyclopedia reference chapter / narrative overview with a 'Further Reading' list. It reports no empirical methodology, no primary data collection, and no systematic empirical synthesis, instead summarizing secondary government statistics and previously published environmental contamination and health studies. Excluded under E05.
criterion_notes.c4: Does not evaluate or report an empirical study outcome measuring water or sanitation access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion; only cites secondary descriptive coverage statistics as background to diarrheal disease burden.
criterion_notes.c5: Because the text is a broad narrative encyclopedia entry rather than an empirical study or systematic synthesis, there is no identifiable empirical study design, analytical sample/unit of analysis, legal/governance exposure, or access outcome.

evidence_quotes.quote: Inadequate sanitation and water supply are major factors implicated in the environmental burden of disease. Only 67% of Ugandan households had access to safe water at the beginning of this decade.
In Kampala City, only 55% of the population has access to piped water, out of which only 9% is connected to the sewerage system.
An example of cross-sectoral involvements has been the national water policy for Uganda, prepared in 1996 to manage and develop the water resources of Uganda in an integrated and sustainable manner.
However, facilitation of environment management activities, including law enforcement and public awareness, and information and training programs, needs emphasis.

raw_response.rationale: This 2011 Elsevier reference/encyclopedia chapter ('Uganda: Environmental Health Concerns') is a broad narrative overview of environmental health hazards and policies in Uganda—focusing primarily on malaria, respiratory conditions, waterborne/parasitic diseases, solid waste, industrial effluent, leaded petrol air pollution, heavy-metal contamination of urban soils and crops, climate change, and general environmental/food-safety legislation—with a 'Further Reading' section and no empirical study design, primary data, or systematic review methodology (E05). In addition, it neither examines household/community water or sanitation service access as a study outcome nor analyses any legal, administrative, or rule-type governance mechanism governing water or sanitation access under either the plain or narrow 2026-10-13 reading of Criterion 2.
